body.text: This past September, theatres rolled a fan favorite back onto the screen for one last hurrah. Avengers Endgame: Encore was released by Marvel as "The epic conclusion to the Infinity Saga", intending it to be the final movie to join the famous 8-year long series. While originally thought of as a simple re- release for fans to enjoy in theatres, it was later revealed that Encore would include extra, never seen before, footage of the film. This excited fans while also bringing into question whether it was worth it to spend money on a ticket to just see a few minutes of extra scenes.
As a longtime fan of Marvel and the Avengers series, senior Mihirr Malhotra remarked, "I was super hype, I was like more scenes? No way!".

His reaction was shared by fans worldwide, many who just appreciated the chance to be back in the world they loved again. With a legacy as famous as the one that the Avengers saga holds, it was impossible that the movie wouldn't gain at least some traction.

Other fans were conflicted on whether they wanted to go or not, junior Shine Duffee recalled, "When I saw it came out, I got really influenced by my friends to go see it. Though, the tickets were a bit expensive to just go watch some extra clips that I could just search up on YouTube later."
This opinion was quite common, with costs skyrocketing, buying a ticket to re-watch a movie simply didn't seem to be worth it or in the budget for a lot of fans.
Alternativity, some people looked down on the act. Bellevue's very own AP Government teacher, Mr. Linser. commented, "Seemed like a money grab to me".
He's not the only one. Gaining more revenue from a movie that's already hit the charts globally didn't seem necessary to critics, an opinion they made vocal following the week Encore premiered.

Ultimately, the release of Avengers Endgame: Encore was a success and grossed approximately $126 million globally. Though it brought some controversy along with it, the re-release ended up being a great chance to see a fan favorite back in the theatres.

body.text: I doubt that most people were able to get to know all the new clubs at Bellevue High School on Tuesday just from the club fair, which is unfortunate since there are dozens of unique and fantastic ones. Some are newer than others and much less known than others. After taking a quick look at various newly approved clubs at BHS, I handpicked four of the most intriguing ones to interview. These are clubs I thought may be hidden gems, less known and understood by the public. And the founder of a club with a niche club name, I thought it would certainly help both the club officers and students to better know what opportunities are around us.
1) Bright Hearts Initiative (third Monday each month, 3:30 in room 2112)
I was a bit confused with the name, so I’ll just have the founder, Chloe Carson, explain it.

“We’re planning on encouragement cards and care packages for kids in hospitals, organizing volunteering opportunities and fundraising,” says Carson. “Our goal is to turn small acts of kindness into actual, meaningful impact.”

Initially, I was skeptical of the uniqueness of the club, as it seemed like just a vague concept. But Carson says that a lot of people want to spread kindness and help others, but a lack of opportunities discourages them. While I believe there is never a lack of opportunities for kindness, they often hide in plain sight. There’s no excuse to be self-centered with the Bright Hearts Initiative. Sometimes we think just sending cards won’t mean anything, but we struggle to understand the circumstances of people truly in hardship. When life seems so bent against you, even a word of compassion could mean the world.
2) Founder’s Club (biweekly on Thursdays, 3:30 in room 0108)

When my father forced me to read Steve Jobs’s biography, it made me want to be an entrepreneur, but not because I wanted to change the world. I was just thoroughly disappointed with the payroll of most conventional jobs. Whether you have a great idea you want to bring to the world or is simply like me, Founder’s club might be for you.

“Founders Club is a startup club, kind of like Y Combinator for high schoolers,” founder (get it?) Arham Bhandari says. “Members build a real business, app, website, or passion project with AI tools.”
But it’s not just your typical club for unserious hobbyists. The major event called Pitch Night at the end of each year gathers investors, and the members with the best project can win $1,000.
“We bring in industry professionals as mentors who give real guidance and networking. We also encourage members to enter competitions,” says Bhandari.

And for high schoolers who place getting into a prestigious college as their top goal in life (not healthy, guys), this provides an opportunity for you to show that you aren’t just a dreamer. You’ve made something of your own, and it could be published or even make you money. You can say that you’ve got what it takes to succeed in the real world, because you’ll learn what you can’t in a syllabus.
3) Fencing Club (every Thursday, 3:30 in room 1121)
As intriguing as fencing club is, one unfortunately might not be able to actually fence on a weekly basis.
“I’m going to have to talk a little with ASB about what I can and can’t do, but probably more events like the [fencing] assembly last year” says founder Jaelynn Shin.

There’s also going to be tournaments outside of school which you could sign up through the club. But usually, they’ll teach some simple techniques and the history behind fencing. And while it might not help you defeat a robber, it could help you sidestep obstructions in the hallways with meticulous footwork. But isn’t it quite dangerous?
“Fencing is actually really safe,” Shin says. “We have a lot of protective gear, but even if we aren’t allowed gear, we can spar with pool noodles.”

Countless professionals dedicate their lives to fencing, and Shin is an example of that, having taken a whole year off in freshman year to pursue this career. But even as a hobbyist, a sport like fencing provides coordination, problem solving skills, and just a whole lot of fun. My house has a traditional Chinese prop sword, so I might bring it to the club one day.
4) American Lung Cancer Screening Initiative (Fridays, 3:30 in room 1116)
This may be the most specific and niche sounding club I’ve heard of, but clearly they’ve been passed by ASB for good reason.
“We encourage at-risk people to get screened for lung cancer, the deadliest cancer in America,” says founder Mona Ayoubzadeh-Bartos.

But high schoolers certainly don’t need to be screened for cancer, right? Bartos says no. That is why members get to spread awareness through posters, social media, and talking to relatives, and instead. There are no barriers to entry, but so many opportunities await. Already in planning are collaborations with UW students, talks by professionals, and internships in outreach events.
“Talking to just one person could possibly save a life,” says Bartos.

Usually, the clubs we hear about are either long-established ones like DECA or those who tell us exactly what they do: aerospace, Muslim culture, physics, etc. But sometimes, the most niche clubs are the most down-to-earth and most engaging. The four new clubs I happened to find intriguing are just a subset of dozens, and they’re filled with determination. I trust that there are many more equally fascinating clubs across the school. Explore activities and give them a chance to impress you. I’m excited to see how they will develop in the coming months, and you should too.

body.text: The Barque has a long track record of sending its alums to prestigious universities, and last year’s class was no exception, with every graduating senior going on to college. Two of those graduates, however, took very different paths. Stella O’Connor chose to stay close to home and enroll in the University of Washington’s Foster School of Business. At the same time, Yash Kothari crossed an ocean to study history at the University of Oxford in England. What does life look like for them in college now?

O’Connor chose the University of Washington for its highly ranked business school, where she is majoring in business administration. Even as an in-state student, she found the move bigger than she expected.
“I thought I was going to feel like I’m at home,” O’Connor said. “It feels so much different.”

One of the biggest changes has been her schedule. In high school, she had six- to seven-hour long school days. Now she usually has one or two two-hour classes a day allowing much more freedom in her schedule.

“Obviously everyone knows that you have more freedom in college,” O’Connor said, “but it’s more than I thought it would be.” The workload surprised her too. “In high school, everyone says that college is going to be super hard,” she said. “But it’s not that hard.”
Outside of class, O’Connor joined the sorority Kappa Alpha Theta. She says her favorite part of college so far has been building a new social circle and meeting new friends.

Overseas, Yash Kothari is in Oxfordshire, England, studying at the University of Oxford. Kothari has had an incredible time in England learning about the social norms, experiencing the culture and navigating academics at an ultra-prestigious university. The move has been extremely insightful for him and has pushed him to reflect on his time at Bellevue High School.

“I didn’t really notice what privilege I had until I graduated from Bellevue. There is so much opportunity and support within the community, and I fully believe it is one of the best academic ecosystems you can grow up in,” Kothari said.
Leaving home was more than just moving to college; it has helped put into perspective how fortunate he was to grow up with so much opportunity.
On campus, Kothari joined Oxford’s newspaper, the Oxford Student, and aims to compete on the university’s debate team.

Kothari is at a centuries-old university an ocean away, and O’Connor is just across Lake Washington. But both found that college was different from what they expected, and both are learning things that high school didn’t teach them. For the seniors in Bellevue’s halls now, their stories and experiences prove that the end of high school is the beginning of change.

articles.title: College Tours are Horrible
articles.author: Zia Shaikh
articles.excerpt: College visits are often listed right at the top of to-do lists for incoming seniors and juniors. Advocates of this practice often say that it’s vital for students to visit the college they are applying for, in order to understand exactly what the college offers in terms of campus, social life and physical infrastructure. Unfortunately, in today’s world, college tours seem to be the latest innovat

body.caption: Scenery of Fordham University during Zia's visit. All photos by Zia Shaikh.

body.text: College visits are often listed right at the top of to-do lists for incoming seniors and juniors. Advocates of this practice often say that it’s vital for students to visit the college they are applying for, in order to understand exactly what the college offers in terms of campus, social life and physical infrastructure.

Unfortunately, in today’s world, college tours seem to be the latest innovation in late stage capitalism where schools attempt to sell you the school rather than show you what it means to live there for the next 4 years. When I went to visit colleges in New York, I found the campus tours showed me shockingly little of the college campus. At Fordham University, the college tour guide showed us to the cafeteria, where they remarked that the University no longer had horrible food. Unfortunately, this was far from the truth, and the University was hiding their food. Additionally, nothing in the tour taught me of the research and internship opportunities within the school. To make matters worse, very little time was set aside in the 4 tours I visited that showed me what academic daily life would uniquely look like in each university.

body.caption: Scenery at Colombia University during Zia's visit.

body.text: However, other students still see the benefit in these pointless visits.
“Actually being on campus can help you make application decisions. The oat milk matcha latte from Rice University's coffeehouse was just another reason for me to apply." Says senior William Liu.

Unfortunately, students like Liu don’t understand that this is the point of college tours. They entice you with matcha and frappucinos, in order to pull wool over your eyes. The real things they are hiding are the ones most important to you. For example, at Cornell University, there is almost nothing referring to the admissions processes, or even specific programs that are accessible for students, specifically related to their major.

Additionally, as a result of university policies, the majority of these tours do not allow for tour guides to be frank about specific policies that the University implements, and the true reality of collegiate life. Although this is to be expected, it does leave a lot on the table in terms of actual understanding of the University.

body.caption: Cornell's track and field stadium during Zia's visit.

body.text: Additionally, college tours remind students about the never ending dread they will experience, separated away from their parents as full fledged adults.

“College tours remind me that I have to be an adult soon." says senior Alex Blacker. The verdict is obvious: if you want to be forced to grow up, sipping matchas and receiving indoctrinated education about your future college, go on a visit. If you want to stay in the real world, but also not become an adult, just stay home.

body.text: Bellevue now has another go-to after-school option for students. OAKBERRY, a new popular açaí restaurant with over 1000 locations worldwide, has now opened in downtown Bellevue. This is the first time an international açaí chain has arrived in Washingtons, bringing its customizable açaí bowls and smoothies.

OAKBERRY offers smoothies and açaí bowls you can personalize with toppings such as granola and fruit. Since açaí bowls have become a popular snack among teens, the restaurant has already caught the attention of Bellevue High School students.
“I think OAKBERRY is going to be really popular with Bellevue students because açaí bowls are such a popular snack right now, and there really good,” junior Alexis Farringer said.
For many students, OAKBERRY offers a lot more than just food: It’s a new downtown location to provide a place to meet friends, connect, and even study after a long, busy day at school.

In addition to giving students a new place to hang out, OAKBERRY also has provided jobs for local students, like senior Olivia Anderson, who works there. When asked about her experience working there since it opened, Anderson shared what she enjoys most about the job.
“My favorite part of working there is getting to talk to all the customers that come through and making different fun acai bowls.”

While downtown Bellevue has many cafés, fast food restaurants, and coffee shops, OAKBERRY brings something new with its customizable smoothies and açaí bowls. The restaurant offers students something different from the usual choices.

OAKBERRY may be popular with students looking for a quick snack or a place to meet up with friends. As more students try OAKBERRY, it will be up to them to decide whether it becomes a place they visit after school or just a place to try once.

body.text: Fresh off his 3rd studio album, alternative R&B artist Steve Lacy has been riding a wave of popularity and recognition. The album’s title track “Oh Yeah” has gone viral after its feature in the smash hit “Spider Man: Brand New Day”, reaching a peak of 19 on the billboard top 100 chart. Still, there is more to Lacy’s discography than many realize.

Although some may recall his earlier breakout track “Bad Habit” in 2022, Lacy’s journey as an artist started in high school as the lead guitarist of Grammy nominated band “The Internet”. Only two years later, Lacy produced the entire song series “Demo” singing into his iPhone mic, composing his own guitar and bass parts, and programming drum patterns with a music software. Lacy soon secured a deal with label RCA Records and continued to make music. His next album Apollo XII (2019) garnered critical acclaim.
“I like how [Lacy’s] song lyrics are really emotionally authentic, especially in his earlier albums like Apollo. It’s very relaxing to listen to his music,” said junior Lexi Kurakata.

His most well-known album, “Gemini Rights” explores the duality of emotion, which landed Lacy the 2023 Grammy for Best Progressive R&B Album. Some would describe his music as neo soul or funk R&B, but Lacy’ s work has so many facets that it cannot be defined by a single genre. Lacy himself describes his style as plaid, weaving together different influences and ideas into one cohesive fabric.

It makes me glad that Steve Lacy is getting so much more recognition for his music through the media. He has a lot of amazing songs (my personal favorites are ‘static’ and ‘the feeling’) that don’t get recognized as often as they should.

“I love Steve Lacy’s new song ‘nothing’, but my all time favorite is ‘dark red’, said junior Vicky Lin, “I’m super excited to go to his concert with my friends because he is one of my favorite artists.”

For the fans who love his most recent songs, consider taking a listen to some more of his music! No matter whether you are a new fan, or have been following Lacy since his early days, there is surely more fantastic music yet to come.

body.text: It’s a well-known fact that downtown Bellevue has countless boba shops. From the perpetually long line at HeyTea to the authentic background of CHICHA San Chen and Molly Tea, nearly a dozen choices already exist within five miles. So, it’s especially shocking when a new boba place opens up amidst all the competition, and even more so when it replaces a previous competitor.

CILO Lab held its grand opening ceremony in mid-September 2026 and joined The Bellevue Connection’s mix of offices and restaurants. The store has a wide, open-air front facing the plaza, and customers can sit outside in the plaza or inside the store to enjoy their treat. It sits in the spot a previous boba chain—Don’t Yell at Me—had occupied for over two years. Though, unlike its predecessor, CILO Lab isn’t strictly a boba store. It adds a certain twist to its menu.

body.caption: Photo by Aimee

body.text: The main attractions at CILO Lab are undoubtedly its gelato and milk teas. Any drink can become a float by adding a scoop of gelato, and the names of the gelatos, namely “Duck Shit,” are unique and eye-catching.
Junior Josephine Chen and I decided to get the Crème Brûlée Fresh Milk Tea and the Uji Matcha Smoothie. Unfortunately, their best-selling drink, the Biscoff Cookie Fresh Milk Tea, was out of stock.

body.caption: Creme Brulee Milk Tea (right) and Uji Matcha Smoothie (left). photo by Josephine

body.text: “The Uji Matcha was really visually appealing with good texture, but it tasted a bit watered down… that might be due to me choosing the sugar free option though,” Chen said.

The gelato was a unique blend of creamy and fruity flavors mixed with a rich tea taste. The Jasmine Cloud gelato is a top seller and is fancy break from the typical strawberry or chocolate flavors seen at most gelato stores.
“Who knew that tea tastes so good with gelato? It’s not fresh-churned, top tier gelato but it’s also not too sweet and pretty good,” Chen said.

body.caption: Jasmine Cloud gelato. Photo by Aimee

body.text: Overall, CILO Lab is a type of boba store that’s never been seen before in the Bellevue area, blending milk tea, gelato and matcha. Its gelato flavors are a must-try, since they aren’t found anywhere else in downtown Bellevue, though for quality boba it might be a better idea to head to a more specialized shop like CHICHA.

Even though it’s a familiar recipe, the drink has taken the public by storm with long lines forming outside every Starbucks around the countr

body.caption: Starbuck's viral unicorn frappuccino drink from Forbes: https://www.forbes.com/sites/ronaldholden/2017/04/18/how-to-catch-the-starbucks-unicorn-elusive-frappuccino-debuts-tomorrow/ .

body.text: This summer, Starbucks relaunched their Unicorn Frappuccino after its initial release in 2017. This viral beverage is crème-based and features a sweet and tart-mango flavored syrup, a tangy blue drizzle, whipped cream, and pink and blue sour powder toppings. Even though it’s a familiar recipe, the drink has taken the public by storm with long lines forming outside every Starbucks around the country. Furthermore, the drink’s unicorn-like appearance, attracted influencers looking to get content for their social media platforms. Due to this surge, the drink quickly turned into an object of overconsumption, with heaps of partially finished drinks overflowing trash cans outside many Starbucks locations.

Although the aesthetic of the Frappuccino is pleasing, many people have reported that the taste does not live up to the presentation of the drink, which is the reason why barely touched drinks are thrown away after a few sips.

Students at Bellevue High claim that the drink tastes somewhat acidic, with sudden spikes in its sour and sweetness levels. Many others have stated that the entire concoction tastes vile and the hype for it is most definitely overrated.
“It tasted very weird, almost a metallic like sour flavor” said senior Saya Toth.

The hype that followed the drink’s release quickly fell when people started to post honest reviews about its mediocrity on social media. The Frappuccino’s rapid decline in reputation highlights how the drink only remained relevant due to its connection with conformity and overconsumption- people were spending money on this drink only because everyone else was. The large amounts of drinks purchased after long hours of standing in line signals how easy it is for people to fall victim to the craze for something as trivial as a drink.

body.text: Every fall at Bellevue the most exciting event is the homecoming dance. What’s even better is the homecoming football game the day before, which features cheerleaders, the band, food trucks and our talented players dominating the field.
Two days before the 2026 hoco game, Hazen High School forfeited the match when too many players became injured or ill, giving girls’ soccer an opportunity to be the central focus for the celebration.

Because of this sudden change, some students have opted to not attend the game, some saying they preferred not to watch girls’ soccer and others becoming visibly upset because of the absence of the male football players.
“Boys are biologically faster than girls which is why football has more attention, is more popular, and better funded,” an anonymous sophomore stated.

This viewpoint may have led to the idea that the girls’ soccer team would not perform as well, solely because they don’t run as fast as the footballers. However, the defending state champion girls’ soccer team defiantly proved this wrong with their performance on game day.

With only one day prior notice, the team trained hard and put all their focus into preparing for the last-minute match. Within the first two minutes, Mackenzie Tucker already scored the first goal and the stadium erupted into applause. Moments before halftime, an impressive shot from Ava Jeremiah at 35 yards flew into the far corner of the net, raising the score to 3-0.

In the 72nd minute, Elle Koszorus headed the ball, aiming towards the back post and straight into the net. After a hard fought match, the final score comes out to be a 6 point win against the Newport girls.
“I never watched soccer before the game, but after I saw how well the girls performed that night, I started to become more interested in the sport,” added sophomore Melinda Zhang.

The supportive audience gave the team a newfound sense of confidence as they walked off the field victoriously. Not only had soccer become the main attraction, but it also gave students the realization that girls’ soccer had the talent and energy to play just as well, if not better than boys’ football.

articles.title: After the World Cup: How to Start Watching Soccer
articles.author: Olivia Myers
articles.excerpt: This summer’s World Cup brought international soccer to Seattle, with 6 matches hosted at Lumen Field. Many Bellevue students attended World Cup games, watched the matches on TV with friends and family, or saw countless videos about the event or the players on social media. For many Bellevue students (including myself), it felt like while the tournament was happening, their summer revolved around

body.caption: Lamine Yamal and his teammates are World Cup champions. Image from Tom Weller/picture-alliance/dpa/AP.

body.text: This summer’s World Cup brought international soccer to Seattle, with 6 matches hosted at Lumen Field. Many Bellevue students attended World Cup games, watched the matches on TV with friends and family, or saw countless videos about the event or the players on social media. For many Bellevue students (including myself), it felt like while the tournament was happening, their summer revolved around when matches were being played each day. But now that the tournament is over, viewers may be wondering what to watch next.
For many, the answer is club soccer, where the same players compete for their club teams year-round.

Soccer differs from traditional American sports in its global scale. Unlike in America where each sport has one main league that is viewed internationally, such as the NBA for basketball and the NFL for football, soccer features a plethora of leagues because each country has one or multiple local leagues for club soccer.
Since sorting through the dozens of leagues that exist for club soccer can be overwhelming, it may be best to start watching matches from one of these three popular leagues.

First is the Premier League in England. In my opinion, this is the best starting point in terms of starting to watch professional soccer. The Premier League is overwhelmingly considered the most competitive league in the world. English soccer dominates international viewership, therefore if your friends or family regularly watch professional soccer, it is likely they watch the Premier League. For that reason, if you enjoy the social aspects of watching sports, such as gathering at a friend's house to watch a game, I suggest starting here. Games air on U.S. weekend mornings and are available to watch on Peacock or USA network. Stars to watch include Norway’s Erling Haaland (Manchester City), England’s Bukayo Saka (Arsenal) and Egypt’s Mohamed Salah (Liverpool).

Junior Ansh Kela watches the Premier League and supports Manchester United. For him, the sport creates personal connections. “What I like about watching soccer is being able to watch games with my dad and getting to make new friends with the same interests,” Kela said.

Similarly to Kela, junior Josie McAughan follows the Premier League. “I like watching the Premier League and my favorite team is Tottenham," she said. "I like when my team wins because it’s once in a blue moon.”

Another popular soccer league that World Cup viewers may enjoy is Spain’s La Liga. Famous for tactical play, heavy possession, and technical skill, La Liga is home to two of the world's biggest sports franchises, Real Madrid and Barcelona, where superstars like Kylian Mbappé and Lamine Yamal play. From my perspective, La Liga is the best choice for viewers who play soccer and want to borrow skills and tactics from the matches they watch to improve their style of play because teams like Barcelona are notably filled with very talented technical players and coaching staff. Matches are available to stream on ESPN on Saturdays and Sundays, however there are occasional weekday games.

Last is the local selection for American fans: MLS (Major League Soccer). This is a great league for Bellevue students to begin watching if they want to go to games in person because Seattle’s MLS team, the Sounders, play about once every two weeks at Lumen Field during the Major League Soccer season.
As one begins to watch soccer, it is important to remember that you don’t need to memorize every rule or roster to start enjoying the sport regularly, the first step is just to watch a game!

body.text: Olivia Rodrigo has brought back her Silver Star Tickets for The Unraveled Tour, giving fans who might not be able to afford regularly priced tickets a cheaper way to see her perform live. The tour for her third album “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl so in Love” began Sep 25 in Hartford and stops at Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle on Dec 7 and 8.
Silver Star tickets cost $20 each, plus a $5 service fee. At $25, Silver Star tickets are far less expensive than regular seats, which can exceed hundreds of dollars for any seat in the arena.

A portion of ticket proceeds goes to Rodrigo’s Fund 4 Good, a global initiative that supports community-based nonprofits working towards girls’ education, reproductive rights, and the prevention of gender-based violence.
“It feels nice to know that the money I’m spending to enjoy her music is going to a good cause,” sophomore Natalie Hang said.

Getting the desired Silver Star tickets requires a different process than purchasing normal concert tickets. Fans submitted a request through Ticketmaster starting Sept 1, but tickets weren’t guaranteed. Ticketmaster said fans would hear back by September 9 on whether they got these limited tickets.
“I’ve always loved her and I was really sad that none of my requests weren’t successful. I haven’t even heard about a single person who got a successful request,” Hang said, after results came out.

Although Silver Start tickets are limited, Rodrigo implemented policies to make sure the process was as equitable as possible. Since tickets are handed out on show day, buyers never get a ticket they could resell ahead of time. The tickets have allowed for a broader audience that may not be able to afford luxuries like concert tickets to enjoy their favorite artist live and support a good cause.

articles.author: Heather Wong

Beginning August 16 th , AMC and Dolby Cinemas partnered to release a limited-edition 10 th anniversary screening, gaining huge success in box offices. La La Land was the top-grossing Oscar movie of 2016 (the year of its initial release) with a total revenue of $340.5 million worldwide ac

body.caption: La La Land 10th Anniversary Poster from Lionsgate.

body.text: With new releases flooding theaters over the last few months, one movie has cut deep into nostalgic territory. Beginning August 16 th , AMC and Dolby Cinemas partnered to release a limited-edition 10 th anniversary screening, gaining huge success in box offices. La La Land was the top-grossing Oscar movie of 2016 (the year of its initial release) with a total revenue of $340.5 million worldwide according to Forbes. Now, as movie theaters across the nation struggle to fill seats, many are left wondering how this 10-year-old film still resonates with moviegoers.

Set in Hollywood, La La Land follows the life of a young jazz musician (Gosling) and an aspiring actor (Stone) chasing after their own dreams—and each other. The two discover how much they must sacrifice to continue their individual pursuits and support one another, ultimately leading to the famous open-ended “what if” conclusion.

Among younger audiences, social media has played a major role in boosting the popularity of La La Land . The musical has recently gone viral with global fans, particularly for its bold color palettes and catchy soundtrack seen in cinematic edits and piano covers.
“As Mia and Sebastian grow closer, the colors they wear become more compatible,” said Junior Amy Zhang. “When they’re more distant, the colors contrast.”

Analysis videos and commentaries praise Damien Chazelle for his award-winning directing skills which brought the film’s artistry and score together. However, critics argue that without such effects, the plot and chemistry of the couple seem less impressive.

According to fans, La La Land has already been widely celebrated and conversation-evoking across streaming platforms, further begging the question: why did cinema companies bring it back to the big screen?
“I would appreciate seeing older movies being brought back to theaters, so I think any rescreening is worth it including La La Land ,” said percussion teacher Mr. Hill.

Still, not all rescreenings guarantee high ticket sale rates. Seasonal or anniversary film screenings aren’t a new concept in local theaters, with Cinemark Classics and AMC’s Fan Faves releases that retell timeless stories. Yet La La Land touches on the reality of balancing a dream career and a serious relationship, continuing to resonate with audiences today.
So, whether you’ve seen the full two-hour film or a five-second clip on Reels, the legacy of La La Land undoubtedly lives on.

body.caption: Image of makee desserts by Vidula Rajesh.

body.text: Are you looking for a new place to get dessert? Well look no further. Taking the place of Sugar & Flake, Makkee is a Chinese dessert chain located right next to Bellevue High School and Voodoo doughnuts. They specialize in traditional Chinese dessert soups such as tangshui (a sweet soup served at the end of meals). Three dishes in particular give an excellent, delicious snapshot of what Makkee has to offer.

Mango Pomelo Sago: This dish features a cold mango smoothie base was packed with frozen mango chunks, sago pearls, and shredded pomelo. The textures went together perfectly since the frozen mango made the bite feel like ice cream mixed sago’s unique chew. The pomelo cut down on the richness of the desert offering a slightly tart aspect that made the combination just right.

Mango, Snow, and Black Sticky Rice: This dish features frozen mango, black sticky rice, and vanilla ice cream on a bed of milky ice. All of the flavors balance each other beautifully: mango adding freshness, ice cream offering creaminess and sweetness, and the rice giving some earthy and nutty notes that make for an amazing flavor experience. The textures here (especially the rice) are addicting, leaving you to want to take another bite.

Mango with Mini Rice Balls: This has the same base as the Mango Sago. It includes frozen mango, mango popping boba, and mini mochi balls. The mango flavor is extremely pronounced here which is delicious. The boba as well as the mochi balls give excellent texture. The burst of flavor and chewiness combined with the cold frozen mango is excellent.

Visiting the shop, all of these amazing deserts were visually stunning. Seeing how well put together they were and how all aspects of the dish played into the visual only made it more appetizing. I spent around $40 for three items, which is around $13.50 per item. The portions were not too filling which is good for a dessert place as many people usually go after meals. for a specialized desert shop I’d say it’s the worth money. if you’re looking to add a new tasty and fun place for a sweet treat, For long lunches, dessert, or a late night ice cream run; Makkee is worth it.

body.text: What’s more stressful than planning HOCO? Finding the perfect dress! Dress shopping requires an enormous amount of preparation. First, most of the dresses ordered online take weeks to arrive, not even considering if the dress fits right or if it looks how you expected. This requires even more planning for exchange time. There is also the issue of finding something in your size, since most schools have HOCO, and sorority rush occurring at the same time; sizes go quickly. The most frustrating part is finding a store that actually accepts returns versus that awful store credit that feels like you are just wasting your money. Here are some tips Bellevue girls have learned along the way to make the process as enjoyable as possible.

Stick to places that offer free shipping and easy, free returns. Revolve and Nordstrom are two of the top contenders. Both send you a free return label, neither cares why you are returning the item (of course, tags need to be on, and it can’t be worn) and they credit you back the same way you paid. Both online retailers have tons of dresses to choose from, and plenty of inventory if the first five dresses don’t work!

Peppermayo is also a popular site many choose to buy dresses from, but customers should be wary of scammer websites. Some have accidentally ordered off “Peppamayo” and “Peepermayo”, only to realize a few typos can end in no dress and your money gone. If you do it the right way though, you can get exactly what you want.
“My dress is from Peppermayo; it came just how I imagined and fits perfectly. I can’t wait to wear it on HOCO!” says junior Hailey Andersen.
Beginning Boutique has a variety of different dresses, with something for everyone. Beginning Boutique does a nice job offering what most students are looking for in a HOCO dress.
“I got my HOCO dress from Beginning Boutique! They have so many cute options, and I fell in love with mine as soon as I saw it!” says junior Stephany Peixoto.

HOCO dress shopping can be stressful if you don’t put some thought into it first. Just remember to give yourself plenty of time to get the rejects back and the next shipment in. Read the fine print when it comes to the cost of the return and whether they even accept returns. And most importantly, pick what makes you feel good, not what’s expected; there is a perfect dress for everyone.

body.text: At noon from Monday to Friday, the H Mart in Main Street Marketplace becomes noticeably busier as the restaurant becomes teeming with a different kind of customer: hungry high schoolers. H Mart is almost BHS’s designated lunch spot. H Mart offers a globally diverse and cheap selection and is within walking distance of the school. However, with such a large selection, choosing what to buy becomes a surprisingly difficult task. But be indecisive no further! Try some of these items the next time you stop for a visit.

This discussion evaluates two qualities of an item: taste and cost. Items that score well in both categories are the true unicorn finds of H Mart. Having personally recommended my finds to friends to great success, here is my list of the must-buy items at H Mart to satisfy both the stomach and the wallet, along with a popular buy to avoid:
1. Spicy Rice Cakes: H Mart’s take on tteokbokki

Tucked away at the far-right end of H Mart’s food court, this easy-to-overlook gastronomic masterpiece lies neatly stacked up. While unassuming reddish orange plastic containers are less appealing than the other beautifully presented selections, just one look at the price already justifies its ranking on the list. For just $3.99, you get a stuffed container filled with rice cakes and Korean fish cakes coated in a thick sweet and spicy broth. H Mart also offers a version with a hard-boiled egg for an extra dollar and a larger version with a taller container. However, the cheapest $3.99 version is always my go-to for cost and amount of food.
2. Vietnamese spring roll: an underrated filler

Vietnamese cuisine is one of my all-time favorites, so I was immediately excited to spot these spring rolls offered. If you’ve ever been to a Vietnamese place, you’ve probably seen these iconic uncooked spring rolls filled with fresh vegetables, herbs, rice vermicelli, and wrapped in translucent sticky rice paper. H Mart’s take on these spring rolls, however, is likely different from what you’ll get at your local pho restaurant, but that’s okay! These spring rolls are larger than typical and filled with more vegetables and herbs than typically and the sauce is more diluted.
3. Bibimbap Triangles: the best grab & go snack

These seaweed-covered, rice-filled triangles stuffed with different fillings are all yours for just $3.99. Out of the different offerings of filling including beef, tuna, and kimchi, my undisputed top pick is the crab. Although the crab is a substitute, the sweet strands of imitation crab adds immense flavor to the surrounding rice in a way that doesn’t make the combination taste dry, a problem that occurs with the other bibimbap triangles. These are easily carried in hand and can be easily eaten on a walk or standing up.
4. Korean-style Fried Chicken: a classic reimagined

This box of Korean-style fried chicken is not what you’ll get at your local fried chicken joint. This chicken is light, airy and crunchy, and I commonly find myself walking out with a box between my hands. H Mart recently raised their prices on this item by around a dollar to $7.99, but this large container of fried chicken is still a worthwhile buy for anyone seeking a delicious treat.
5. Rice bowls are overpriced

H Mart’s signature bowls of rice, usually accompanied with some selection of protein are always presented neatly stacked in their black packaging and put on display under the lights of the hot foods display. While they seem enticing, I’ve come to learn that the entire bowl quickly becomes stale and loses its appeal near the end. Besides, they consistently hover around the $12 to $15, a steep price to be paying compared to the other items on this list.

body.caption: A photogenic early rise the morning of NOF 2026 in San Francisco with BHS Chamber Orchestra. Image by Evan Du

body.text: In late April, Chamber orchestra (the most advanced ensemble here at BHS) received word that they had been accepted to the National Orchestra Festival for the second year running. NOF is one of the top orchestra conferences in the nation, and even being admitted is an accomplishment. It took months of preparation and rehearsal beforehand to submit the best possible application. Last year, Chamber was lifted from the waitlist into the non-competitive track. But this year, they were accepted directly into the competitive division and earned higher ratings by adjudicators on the audition recording, reflecting tremendous growth. Orchestra director Andrew Kam couldn’t be prouder.
“It’s a huge accomplishment. It took years of building rehearsal culture, performance expectations, and even attendance,” Kam said.
But such an accomplishment doesn’t come easily. There’s a lot going on under the surface that most will never see.

“What most people don't realize - is that we don't necessarily need the best musicians or instrumentalists to have a successful group - we need students who stay humble and are constantly pursuing growth. Audiences may not see the huge amount of selflessness it takes for a group to work together. Students of all levels and age have to learn to put the needs of others in front of themselves. In some cases this is a big ask - maybe there's a huge test next class, or something very personal is happening in their lives. The trick is to balance how we care for ourselves, and how we care for others, particularly when time doesn't stop, and we have a concert coming up with limited rehearsal time,” Kam said.
Big things lay ahead for orchestra. Notably, large enrollment.

“The growth of this program cannot be understated. Our enrollment has skyrocketed from 80 in Fall 2018, to 170 Fall 2026. Having a larger orchestra membership can mean students are working harder than ever to put themselves in leadership roles either musically, organizationally, or both. Even our ORCO (orchestra council) has elevated the student experience. We used to have a team of 3, and now out of necessity we have a team of 6 council students to support the 150+ students we had this year,” Kam said.

Many feel as if this year’s qualification for NOF was a milestone and a breakthrough for orchestra. Representing our school and orchestra at the national level is a big deal. Kam hopes orchestra stays humble and continues to grow.

“I would love for Chamber Orchestra to apply to Mid West Clinic and/or Orchestra Cup in New York,” Kam said. “Like NOF, both are prestigious merit-based festivals which are among the most competitive in the country.”
Kam also has high aspirations for the orchestra’s second-highest group, the non-audition Sinfonia orchestra.
“I also want to present Sinfonia at either State Conference or All-Northwest Conference,” he added. “The more merit-based opportunities earned for our program, the better.”
Though despite the accolades, he gave a reminder to not forget what comes first:
“Most importantly, I hope all our orchestra students lead by example and practice citizenship, musicianship and friendship.”
Kam finishes off with a heartwarming message to orchestra students:

“Huge shoutout to all my students. Without them, there is no orchestra. I'm sorry my jokes are really bad in class, but I cannot express how grateful I am that I can be myself in front of you all. Chicago 2027 and Disneyland 2027! LG!!!”

In fact, just last year 8,824 new TV shows were filmed according to SG Einwatchter, a professor at Aalborg University. Among the thousands vying for eyes only a select few are able to

body.caption: Invincible seen in his signature blue and yellow fists towards the audience. Illustration by Oz Galeano.

body.text: While TV is often seen as a dying medium, many studios would beg to differ, while Youtube and Tiktok dominate media consumption, studios around the world are still pouring billions of dollars a year into television. In fact, just last year 8,824 new TV shows were filmed according to SG Einwatchter, a professor at Aalborg University. Among the thousands vying for eyes only a select few are able to catch audiences attention, and in recent years “Invincible” has captivated audiences. Season 4 released in March of this year, has 4/8 episodes awarded IMDb’s prestigious “Top Rated” title.

So does the season actually live up to the hype? For the most part, absolutely. Premiering on Prime Video on March 18th with a three episode drop and weekly releases after, season 4 picks up with Mark Grayson in the worst shape we have ever seen him. After the devastation of the Invincible War and his brutal fight with Conquest, Mark is haunted by the lives he could not save, and the show is not afraid to sit in that darkness. New villain Dinosaurus is introduced early on, and while he is not throwing the biggest punches yet, he forces Mark to confront an uncomfortable question: would killing his enemies actually save more lives? It is heavy stuff for a cartoon, and that is exactly why Invincible works.

The animation, long a sore spot for some fans, is noticeably more ambitious this time around, and the action is bloodier and more frequent than any previous season. Critics have taken notice too. That said, many at Bellevue don’t seem to mind the animation quality, Sophomore Denny Lemme, says “The animation is fine especially with the timeline the animators were put on, honestly, it doesn’t really matter at all to me.” Many seemed to agree with this sentiment as season 4 debuted with a perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes, continuing the streak set by seasons 2 and 3, with reviewers calling it arguably the best superhero show on television right now and praising how it finally brings the long teased war to Viltrum itself, raising the stakes to a truly cosmic level.

That said, the season is not flawless. Episode 4, a detour where Mark travels to hell to help Damian Darkblood reclaim Satan's throne, is easily the low point. The storyline was invented for the show rather than adapted from the comics, and it shows, dragging the pacing right when momentum matters most. Some viewers will also find the middle stretch a bit overstuffed with side plots.

Still, these are minor stumbles in an otherwise phenomenal run. The finale refuses easy resolutions, instead setting up an even bigger conflict that promises to reshape the entire universe of the show. Four seasons in, when most series start coasting, Invincible is somehow still climbing. In a year with nearly nine thousand new shows fighting for your attention, this one has more than earned its spot at the top of your watchlist.

body.caption: Movie poster for Poject Hail Mary. I've always wanted to see it. Photo from IMDb.

body.text: When “Project Hail Mary” hit the theaters this in spring, it quickly became an internet sensation.
“I thought the movie was great adaptation of the book. The actors did a phenomenal job, and I really enjoyed watching it with my family,” said senior Milo Blanco.
So, as always, The Barque had to report on it. Down below is our comprehensive review of the movie. As always, stop reading now if you are trying to avoid spoilers!

One of the first problems that “Project Hail Mary” runs into is its beginning. The main character, Ryland Grace, wakes up alone on a spaceship with little memory of who he is, on a mission to save the planet. Now, as someone who read the book, this structure of the beginning concerned me the most. The book is told through first-person narration, where we get to hear Grace’s inner thoughts, which means that even though we still have a limited perspective on what is happening some context still does exist. I didn’t think this would translate well into a movie format. However, despite the doubts I had going in, the movie did an excellent job easing us into the storyline. Scenes where Grace is seen running into trouble dealing with the spaceship or hastily trying to write out everything he knows on a whiteboard illustrates his emotional turmoil without having to spoon-feed lots of monologuing to the audience. Of course, there are a few awkward moments when Grace talks out loud to himself, but they aren’t super noticeable and don’t detract heavily from the movie.

One thing that makes the movie great, however, is its humor. Now, if any other actor was strolling around wearing corny chemistry shirts and cracking sarcastic jokes, I don’t think the humor would have been nearly as solid. But somehow, Ryan Gosling, who plays Grace, is perfect on most of his deliveries every single time. When Grace meets an alien named Rocky, also on a mission to save its plant, a lot of the information we get on his species is told through tiny video clips aboard Grace’s spaceship. The clips are told in a reality TV style format, where Grace does confessionals to the camera about what living with Rocky is like. It adds a sense of humor to the scientific aspects of the movie, which resonated well to me as an audience member.
While this wasn’t a problem for me, some who watched the movie had issues with the second main character, the alien life-form Rocky.
“It was hard for me to empathize with a rock,” said biology teacher Jessica Carruthers.

However, in my opinion, I think Rocky’s unique appearance is part of what makes the movie so good. Typically, in other space movies (like “Star Wars” and “Avatar”), the creatures that are friendly often take on a humanoid form. I thought that Rocky’s rock-like visuals, as well as the difficulties he has in perceiving things in a human way make the movie a little more realistic. After all, it’s very unlikely that the first life we encounter outside of Earth would take a humanoid form.

The best part about the movie, however, is its story of cooperation. The movie centers relationship between Rocky and Grace, and portrayed the emotional exchanges between the two beautifully. The scene where their spaceship breaks and Rocky risks everything to save Grace is so dramatic that it made me tear up in the theater. Likewise, the heart wrenching realization Grace comes to when he realizes he will have to go back and save Rocky is delivered with perfect emotional intent.
“I think one of the best parts of the movie was that it really showed how two organisms so different can come together, find things in common and still build a relationship,” said freshman Jane Lee.

The relationship between Rocky and Grace is one of friendship, where both share their own scientific discoveries together. The innovations that occur as a result illustrate that when scientists of different backgrounds and perspectives work together, it can create life-saving results. That message was one of the things I loved most about the book, and the movie does an excellent job adapting that to the big screen.

Now, if you’re someone who is into the nitty-gritty science of space travel, there are some moments where the movie might fall short. Lots of descriptions of all the scientific explanations that were in the book are cut out from the movie, because the focus is less on the technology and more on the relationships between the characters. For most, this isn’t an issue. However, if you’re someone who loved the book because of how it nerds out about astrophysics, you might leave the theater a little disappointed at what was left out.
“I definitely think the book is better at explaining the scientific stuff, because the movie kind of generalizes it,” Lee said.

Overall, however, I think “Project Hail Mary” would work as a fantastic standalone if it wasn’t an adaption. The raw emotion projected by Gosling onscreen combined with the surreal environment of space creates a fantastic story that immediately sucks the viewer in. So, if you’re looking for your next watch, you might want to stop by Lincoln Square and buy a ticket to go see it while it’s still screening.

body.text: This spring, many bakeries have opened their stores in Bellevue, bringing a spectrum of sweet pastries and aromatic breads. The Bellevue community is incomplete without food businesses, and that’s why The Barque is excited to share a comprehensive review on some of the most popular places for Bellevue High School (BHS) students and the community.

First, one of the students’ favorites is the BA Artisan Bakery just a few blocks away from BHS. They are known for their Rose Bagel and Rose Egg Tart inspired by rose-based pastries in Yunan, China. Additionally, they also offer numerous sourdoughs, Maritozzo, cakes and drinks. The chewiness of the bread, the delicate texture of cakes, the crisp in the egg tart and all the rich flavors make their bakery unforgettable. All their products are promised to be freshly baked daily, and you can see the kitchen filled with busy pastry chefs when you walk into the door. This place is truly a favorite of mine and many other students.

Another popular place for students is Voodoo Donuts, which is even closer to BHS. Many BHS students would go with friends during lunch or after school because of their airy and melt-in-your-mouth goodness and being in an ideal location. If bread and pastries aren’t your favorite type of treat, this may be the place for you.

“I like Voodoo Donuts because it's really unique, and I think their product names are fun! It's a fun place to go with friends and it’s really accessible. My favorite type of donuts there is Marshel Madness,” senior Rainn Reinmiller said.

Located near Bellevue Library, Paris Baguette is a new bakery that is worth the visit. This store opened this spring, and it’s often busy with families and workers around Bellevue. They are known for the flaky and buttery French bakeries, as well as having a large and clean dining space.
“I really like the new café, Paris Baguette, because it has a pretty wide range of pastries, an interesting seasonal menu, and they have a really yummy hotdog bread,” senior Isabella Yang said.
On the other hand, students didn’t respond with similar excitement for L’experience Paris. Although their food and pastry were quite tasty, there are notable issues with their customer service.

"L'experince Paris is utterly disappointing and should not exist due to its terrible customer service. When my friends and I arrived at the store, they said they don’t take reservations even though they confirmed our table for eight at 11:45 a.m. a week beforehand,” senior Kimaya Prasanna Raghavan said.

Last but not least, Tous les Jours is frequently filled with BHS students due to its proximity to school. They offer a very wide selection of bread, pastries and cakes. Some of my personal favorites include their tiramisu, cream-filled donuts and various flavors of croissants. On a side note, Tous les Jours also takes orders for birthday cakes, so if you loved one of their sliced cakes, make sure to check that out.

That’s all for The Barque’s review of Bakeries in Bellevue. If you love food as much as I do, or you simply want a place to hang out with friends, visit these places immediately! The recommended bakeries will not disappoint you.

Kline’s journey at Bellevue

body.caption: David Kline. Photo by Ivy Green.

body.text: The average high school teacher stays at a single school for about seven years . However, Bellevue’s drama teacher, David Kline has spent more than 40 years at Bellevue. In honor of Kline’s remarkable career at Bellevue, which is concluding, we decided to highlight some of his favorite memories during his and hear from some students whose life he has profoundly shaped.
Kline’s journey at Bellevue started in 1986, and, contrary to popular belief, he was actually reluctant to take the job.

“At first I didn’t want to work with kids, because I thought they would be arrogant and bratty. However, when I worked with the students at Bellevue, I realized they were anything but that. The kids were driven, passionate and exceptionally talented.”
In 1988 Kline accepted an offer to become the school’s full time drama director, and he has never looked back since.

Among the countless shows Kline has organized, we asked him to reminisce on some of the most memorable over 40 years. One that immediately came to mind was the first time Bellevue’s drama program went to Scotland in 2013. Here, they performed the play “Return to the Forbidden Planet,” which is a British sci-fi musical. Performing at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival required the group to set up their stage and props, perform the show and tear down the stage and props all in under two hours.

“When we performed, we went through the entire process in an hour and 50 minutes. A recording circulated around YouTube and we became one of the most popular performances of the entire festival,” Kline remarks.

Another memorable show came when the group decided to perform the show “The Laramie Project,” which was a documentary play based on the hate crime killing of Matthew Sheppard, a gay college student in Laramie, Wyoming. Bellevue became one of the first high schools in the entire nation to perform the play. With this controversial show came genuine push back from certain groups.

“A religious group in Missouri protested and actually wrote us mail saying that they would fly over to Seattle, and protest in the auditorium during the play. They actually followed up on this promise, and came to Seattle, but were deterred from coming to play due to our rainy weather,” Kline said.
Throughout his career, Kline hasn’t just directed memorable shows, he has also had a profound impact on his students.

“I started theatre on a whim, randomly auditioning with my friend our freshman year for Dracula. When I was cast alone, I was sure I was going to quit. At our first rehearsal, Kline rushed to make me feel welcome. I have been in every show since,” says senior Caitlin Mochan.

You may be wondering what Kline will do with his free time post retirement. For most, it may seem like the most obvious choice to enjoy a quiet retirement after so many years of teaching. Kline has a different view.
“After I retire, I plan to start writing plays again and go and experience theater in the real world. I want to get back to directing and pursuing drama like the years before I began teaching,”

For Kline, the ending of his career signals the start of another. As he put it, “Every closing night is exciting, because it means there's a chance for another opening night,” a philosophy that defines not only his career, but his entire approach on the stage.

body.text: Summer is just around the corner and it’s the perfect time to get a refreshing acai bowl or smoothie on a hot day. But then comes the difficult decision: where do you go? Bellevue has many delicious selections, and most students are stumped on deciding. A few of highlights include are Matcha Magic, Pressed, Emerald City, Jamba Juice and the newest addition Joe and the Juice. Let’s take a look at our very own students’ fan favorites!

An all-time favorite is Matcha Magic. Matcha Magic is on Main Street which is a close location to grab a bite during lunch. They are known for their matcha, but they also have food such as avocado toast, Nutella toast and acai bowls. They even let you customize your orders to fit your needs!
“Josie Lynch and I love Matcha Magic. My go to order is the uncrustabowl because it has the perfect balance of peanut butter and mix of fruit,” junior Mackenzie Tucker said.
“Matcha Magic is the way to go. The convenient location, preorder and delicious flavors, you just can’t go wrong,” junior Riley Gribble said.

Another fan favorite is Pressed Juice. Pressed not only has juices, acai bowls and smoothies, but they also have froyo. Pressed is a great place if you want to get started on a juice cleanse or want a healthy sweet treat. Also, Pressed is right next to Bellevue Square, making it a quick and easy stop.
“I love to get a sweet treat at Pressed because they are both healthy and sweet. I like to get either the Dubai or S’more’s Froyo, a great combo,” sophomore Cole Pellegrini said.

A new but trendy place is Joe and the Juice which is located in the mall. This is a new addition, and it is already starting to become a hot commodity. Joe and the Juice has delicious sandwiches, tasty coffee, and juices of course.
“I always get a matcha and spicy tuna sandwich because I love it and I don’t want to try anything else,” senior Charlene Stolte said.
Now that you’ve heard all of the best smoothie and acai bowl places in Bellevue, go check out some of them. On a hot summer day, a refreshing acai bowl or thirst-quenching smoothie is the way to go.

Inside are both toothpaste and a toothbrush, because apparently oral hygiene waits for no one. Alongside thos

body.caption: Vansh Chopra with his backpack. Photo by Stella O'Connor.

body.text: Some students carry notebooks. Some students carry folders. Vansh Chopra carries hamsters and sidewalk chalk.
At first glance, his black Lululemon backpack looks normal enough. Then you open it.

The first thing you notice is that Vansh appears to be fully prepared for any dental emergency. Inside are both toothpaste and a toothbrush, because apparently oral hygiene waits for no one. Alongside those are hand sanitizer, lip balm, lemon mints, multiple bottles of eye drops, a timer, a PowerPoint clicker, and a piece of chalk whose purpose remains a mystery.
The next thing you'll notice is what isn't in his backpack.
Folders? None.
Notebooks? None.
Pencil case? None.

Instead, Chopra’s entire academic career seems to be supported by a single binder containing exactly one sheet of paper: notes for AP Lang. While most students spend late August stocking up on school supplies, Vansh appears to have decided that one page was all he really needed.
Then we arrive at the technology section.

Most students carry one school provided laptop. Vansh regularly carries two. For a brief period, this seemed like an unbeatable accomplishment. However, he has officially been surpassed by Teo Tagavilla, who reportedly carries three laptops in his backpack. This has sparked what can only be described as Bellevue's least necessary competition – a fight to see who can carry the most school-issued laptops. And of course, alongside those two laptops Chopra carries four laptop styluses, two for each laptop… obviously! While some students compete in sports, others compete in seeing how many electronics they can fit into a backpack.

To finish things off, Chopra carries a bottle opener keychain dedicated entirely to his Diet Coke habit. Some people carry lucky charms. Some people carry family photos. Chopra carries a tool specifically designed to help him access caffeine.

Overall, Vansh's backpack tells the story of someone who has completely abandoned traditional school supplies. Somehow, despite carrying basically nothing academic except one sheet of paper, along with lugging enough random items around to stock a convenience store, he continues to make it through the school day and is even graduating two years early. Whether that's thanks to preparation or luck is still up for debate.

Each year, roughly 1500 high school teams around the United States compete in the National Science Bowl tournament sponsored by the Department of Energy. But only the top 64 teams are able to compete in finals, meaning that if using this as a mea

body.caption: Left to right (BHS Team 1): Tara Saini, Dhruv Saini, James Huang, Arseni Dzeravianka and Andrew Fu. Standing in front of Congress in DC whilst an excavator tears down establishments, like the state of the country. Photo by Vadzim Dzeravianka.

body.text: For the first time ever, the Bellevue High School Science Bowl team advanced to finals, obtaining a fully paid trip to Washington DC at the end of April. Each year, roughly 1500 high school teams around the United States compete in the National Science Bowl tournament sponsored by the Department of Energy. But only the top 64 teams are able to compete in finals, meaning that if using this as a measure of academic rigor, our school is one of the best in the country.

The lineup for the finalist team, also called BHS Team 1, are juniors Dhruv Saini, his sister Tara Saini, Arseni Dzeravianka, Andrew Fu and alternate James Huang. Each contestant specializes in a combination of topics which include biology, chemistry, Earth and space, physics, energy and astronomy.
“We got the hang of the format and were able to anticipate the types of questions, so we answered faster,” Tara Saini says, explaining why they improved their record drastically.

To reach finals, they first must win the online regionals tournament, beating 19 other teams, including the school Baton Rouge, which qualified for finals in 2024. This is extremely impressive, as Baton Rouge Team 1 defeated the other BHS team (which included me) with a score of 134-20. But with consistent practice with well-timed luck, they were able to pull through.
“There was one time we didn’t know a question about who what the blue LED is made of,” Dzeravianka says. “But Andrew watched a reel and answered it.”

Maybe the lesson to take away is that one can educate themselves by doing anything, even scrolling. Unfortunately, finals were much, much harder. They had to compete against teams like BASIS and Lakeside, the second strongest STEM school in Washington. Thus, the team was unable to win any of the eight round robin games and did not advance to the elimination bracket. In their practices and through the tournament experience, even they expressed disbelief at how competitive the winning teams were.

“We would hear a question involving physics terms we have never heard about, and teams would buzz before hearing the entire question,” Fu says. “the responses were so fast that the auditorium erupted in cheering.”
Nevertheless, the trip to DC was a lot of fun. The teams took several

body.caption: The Air and Space Museum must have been a blast for Fu, the president of BHS aerospace club. Photo by Tara Saini.

body.text: days initially touring landmarks like the air and space museum. Hungry after the flight there, our competitors were surprised by a large buffet for dinner. They also stayed at the same residence, the National Conference Center, where each person received their own room. Clearly, the treatment when funded by the federal government is excellent. Though, the layout of the place, with dozens of winding hallways, could use some improvements.
“We always get lost and keep finding different versions of the same place with slight differences so we can never tell where we are, like the backrooms,” Dhruv Saini said.

BHS Team 1 plans to compete again next year, hoping to achieve even better results. Their story tells us that trying again should not discourage you, and improbable results can be achieved with practice. So, if you want to challenge them, ask to join them or seek out BHS Team 2. No matter where you are right now, you could be the one to finish what they started. Bellevue High might have a chance on the national stage after all.

articles.author: Aimee Ni
articles.excerpt: Starting high school can be tough, especially when you’re a freshman wandering the halls of Bellevue High wondering why the school website does not have digital maps. However, after a year of experience, freshmen now walk the halls with confidence. The class of 2029 has learned a lot, so let's hear about some of their experiences and their advice for the future freshmen who will soon follow in the

body.caption: Photo by Aimee

body.text: Starting high school can be tough, especially when you’re a freshman wandering the halls of Bellevue High wondering why the school website does not have digital maps. However, after a year of experience, freshmen now walk the halls with confidence. The class of 2029 has learned a lot, so let's hear about some of their experiences and their advice for the future freshmen who will soon follow in their footsteps.

A challenge is presented on the very first day upon entering the school: finding the classroom. The BHS building is much larger and complex than what many freshmen are used to in middle school, and even with a map, running around looking at the numbers on the classroom doors is still a tough task.
“On my first day, BHS felt huge and I was honestly scared I'd never find my way around,” freshman Vanisha Brahmbhatt said.
Locating the classes is not the biggest challenge though, some feel that making a new friend is far more nerve wracking.

“On my first day of school I felt really nervous about meeting new people in such a big school,” freshman Elise Dang said. “A challenge I faced this school year was being confident enough to talk to new people for help or just for friendship.”

It can be tough at first, but persevering through the initial hardships are be worth it. Since BHS is a big school there is a place for everyone. The hallways become much more familiar after a few weeks and BHS’s large club selection will help incoming freshmen make many meaningful memories.
“A highlight this year was all the fun I had in my classes and all the school events,” Dang said.
Figuring out everything alone is difficult, so here is what the current freshmen have to say about managing academic work and stress from challenging classes.
“I wish I had known better time management strategies from the start because figuring them out on the fly made my first semester a lot harder than it needed to be,” Brahmbhatt said.

Keeping a planner or using sticky notes to keep track of assignments in every class can be helpful for managing tasks. Otherwise, the increase in workload can feel overwhelming and cause anxiety. Handling stress is important too and managing these emotions are just as important as keeping track of homework.
“I wished I had known… not to stress myself too much about homework and tests and just to balance everything out,” Dang said.

Starting over is never easy, but the challenges these freshmen have faced this year are ones almost every BHS student knows. By now they have overcome these hurdles and look towards another great year with the hardest part behind them. Next year will certainly be another great year for these rising sophomores with wonderful memories to come.

For many students at Bellevue, May means the nearing of AP exams and the subsequent month of studying and rigorous preparation. Known for being college-aligned classes, AP classes often challenge students more than honors classes, with their culminating test an ultimate indicator of a stud

body.caption: Student studying very hard (the light level is not suitable for the eyes). Image from Unsplash by Victor Sutty.

body.text: Contrary to common belief, the month of May doesn’t only bring about spring’s full bloom and cherry blossoms. For many students at Bellevue, May means the nearing of AP exams and the subsequent month of studying and rigorous preparation. Known for being college-aligned classes, AP classes often challenge students more than honors classes, with their culminating test an ultimate indicator of a student’s mastery of the subject. As AP season nears its end, it is valuable for both AP and non-AP students to see what methods people are using to succeed at the AP level.
At the base level, AP students always organize their goals.
“I always create a to-do list of what I want to accomplish when I study. It really helps me gather my thoughts before I go straight into studying,” said sophomore Logan Wong.

Most AP students like Wong prioritize the initial preparation before diving into the work. It makes sense; preparation is key to avoiding overwhelming yourself and to keep track of your studying. Notably, some AP students go further with keeping track.
“I set a timer for 30 minutes. If I get distracted, I pause the timer, making sure that I actually spent the 30 minutes doing work,” said junior Katelyn Wong, who is taking six AP classes this year.

Many AP students highly recommend this strategy. Often, students set a one-hour timer but immediately get off-task, making the amount of time they worked more like 40 minutes rather than the hour they imagined.

Tracking time worked and organizing tasks can prove to be highly effective in ensuring effort. But another important question remains: how do AP students manage the countless amounts of coursework they receive?
“I try to not think about the amount of homework I have. I just focus on what I have ahead of me,” said junior Jimin Baek.
Baek has taken upon four AP classes this year, which has certainly taken a toll on his free time. However, Baek often describes the rigorous effect of APs doesn’t have to be that bad.
“If I were studying, I would view each thing as their own piece. It makes it a lot less overwhelming. Instead of thinking about the whole, focus on the one assignment you’re doing,” Baek furthered.
Even for non-AP students, it’s worthwhile to try these studying methods – they’re tried and true and worth a shot for people worrying about a big test or how to start studying.

body.text: Most students at Bellevue high get their 40 hours of required community service out of the way and don’t think about it again. Many high school students volunteer to put it on their college application, but volunteering can give you experience outside of your daily routine. Volunteering brings a lot of value to students by getting them out of their comfort zone, requiring them to do research, and interacting with adults and children. It helps develop interviewing skills and can help introduce you to a diverse group of community members. The biggest reward is the impact on the community, helping those who are less fortunate, and supporting philanthropies in need.

One way Bellevue High School pushes students to volunteer is the Wolverine Guard PTSA sponsored award that recognizes students for volunteering over 100 hours from May 1 to April 30. It is not an easy award to obtain; a student must carefully track their hours and get them signed off before the cut-off date. Recipients of this award are listed on the Bellevue High PTSA website, and students with two consecutive years of Wolverine Guard receive a special cord to wear at graduation. This award highlights students who spend time giving back to their communities.

Bellevue High School has some favorites when it comes to volunteering. For example, Shirts Across America offers students the chance to go to Alabama and Louisiana in order to learn about social justice and help rebuild homes destroyed by Hurricane Katrina.

“Shirts Across America was great experience for me because it changed my perspective on volunteering and taught me how much of an impact you can make from community service,” says junior Lynzie Schiller.

If you are looking for a local place, a favorite is Bellevue Farmers Market, which runs from May through October. Volunteers assist with vendor set-up, clean, count customers attending the event and take pictures for their social media.
“I like working at Bellevue Farmers Market because I get to interact with customers. I also get to be outside and enjoy the summer weather while volunteering,” said sophomore Saige Haynie.
Jubilee Reach needs volunteers to grocery shop for their food bank, sort groceries and help with their thrift store and daycare activities.
“Volunteering at the thrift store was a great experience because the workers are super supportive and make helping out enjoyable,” says sophomore Lea Trittenbass.
At the end of the day, Wolverine Guard is about stepping up and making a difference. Students looking to get involved can learn more through the Wolverine Guard page on the BHS PTSA website.

body.text: For 27 years and counting, California’s Coachella event has been one of the biggest performances this year in both music and pop culture. With all this excitement, people around the globe tuned in this year to watch all the dynamic performances. From long-awaited performances to standout surprise sets, Bellevue students had a lot to say about the festival’s most memorable moments.

This year, Coachella had people talking more than ever, with headliners including Sabrina Carpenter, Karol G and Justin Bieber, leading some to refer to the event as “Bieberchella.” Bieber returned to the stage as a pop icon, proving that his star power hasn't faded after years away from touring.

“Justin Bieber was the performer I was the most excited for,” said junior Aracely Garcia Mendez, “Even though all he did was screen share his laptop, it was still really exciting to see him perform again and hear his old music.”

In addition to Bieber's highly anticipated set, another headliner that didn't disappoint was Sabrina Carpenter. Labeled "Sabrinawood," her Hollywood-themed spectacle featured cinematic shorts with countless celebrity cameos, including Madonna.
“I really liked Sabrina Carpenter’s performance because of the storytelling,” said sophomore Olivia Myers. “I especially liked weekend two when she brought out Madonna to sing ‘Like a Prayer.’”

As the festival continued, it became clear that Coachella isn't just about the top celebrities. This year, there were over 160 performers at the festival. Both new and seasoned, these performers showed the same level of enthusiasm as the renowned headliners, giving many of their loyal fans something to look forward to. Over the course of the event, there were many notable performances by The Strokes, Addison Rae, Katseye, Young Thug and Ethel Cain.

“I really loved the Ethel Cain set! I saw her live in August, and the stage looked the same,” said freshman Ella Barsuk. “She sang songs from both albums and a few different EPs without autotune or overproduction; it was so pretty!”

Whether students tuned in for Bieber, Carpenter, or smaller artists like Cain, Coachella 2026 gave everyone something to talk about. From major headliners to unexpected standout moments, this year’s festival once again showed why Coachella remains one of the most-watched events in music.
